column1: pii|fix|The Proto-Indo-Iranian period is tied to the Sintashta culture (c. 2050–1900 BCE), so dates were changed to 2100–1700 BCE. Sacred drink *sauma (soma/haoma, probably ephedra), priests, *daywás and *Hasuras, *Hrta (ṛta/aša) and Mitra confirmed. A fire god (*Hagníš) is reconstructed but no specific fire ritual, so the description was reworded.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Indo-Iranian_religion

ivc|ok|Mature phase c. 2600–1900 BCE; undeciphered script; Great Bath possibly ritual; female figurines and the 'Pashupati seal' interpretations are debated or speculative.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indus_Valley_civilisation

jom|part|Jōmon c. 14,000–300 BCE; ornate dogū figurines; burial mounds and grave goods; elements described as precursors of Shinto. Animist and fertility beliefs are inferred and not covered by the checked source.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C5%8Dmon_period

chn|part|Liangzhu (3300–2300 BCE) ritual jade cong and bi, elite burials and the Yaoshan altar confirmed. Bone divination in this period is not covered by the checked source.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liangzhu_culture

sem|fix|Only a generic word for deity, *ʔil-, is reconstructed (later El as a proper name); named sun, moon and storm gods are not confirmed. Proto-Semitic is dated c. 4500–3900 BCE with a disputed homeland, so start moved from 3500 to 4000 BCE and the description was reworded.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Semitic_language

min|ok|Peak sanctuaries, double axe, bull-leaping, snake-goddess figurines (possibly priestesses), and a dominant goddess. Cited sites run from c. 2900 to after 1400 BCE, with Mycenaean conquest c. 1450 BCE.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minoan_religion

ela|ok|Inshushinak (Susa's protector, later head of the supreme triad), Pinikir, Humban and Napirisha; prominent mother goddesses (Kiririsha); Chogha Zanbil as religious capital; civilization c. 3200–539 BCE.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elamite_religion

egp|fix|Naqada I–III c. 3900–2900 BCE; figurines near bodies suggest mortuary ritual; Naqada III grave goods elaborate; first pharaohs and royal motifs (Gebel el-Arak knife). Animal burials are not covered by the checked source, so they were removed from the description.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naqada_culture

pau|part|The 'Out of Taiwan' expansion ran c. 3000–1500 BCE; animism and ancestor effigies confirmed. The reconstructed *qanitu and taboo terms are not covered by the checked portion of the source.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austronesian_religions

dio|fix|Ecstatic wine, music and dance rites open to slaves, women and outsiders; Bacchic gold tablets direct the dead to the Lake of Memory. Attested 5th c. BCE–3rd c. CE, so dates moved from 600 BCE–400 CE to 500 BCE–300 CE.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dionysian_Mysteries
epi|ok|Founded 307 BCE; gods exist but do not intervene; the soul is mortal; ataraxia as the goal; declined by the late 3rd c. CE.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epicureanism

dac|part|Herodotus (before 425 BCE) describes the Getae's belief that the dead go to Zalmoxis and the four-yearly messenger sacrifice; the cult's origin is uncertain. The end date (Roman conquest, 106 CE) is not covered by the checked source.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zalmoxis
sol|ok|Aurelian made Sol Invictus a chief imperial god with a temple dedicated 25 December 274; the last known inscription is from 387.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sol_Invictus

scy|ok|Herodotus names Tabiti (hearth), Papaios (sky father), Api (earth and water), Thagimasadas and Artimpasa; the sword of 'Ares' on a brushwood shrine; horse sacrifice. Of Iranian origin, with possible Ossetian survivals.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scythian_religion

oir|ok|Mithra (covenants), Anahita (waters), the daivas, haoma pressed in the yasna, and sacred fire. Worship took place in the open without images or temples, and the religion was gradually displaced by Zoroastrianism.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Iranian_religion

sib|part|'Shaman' comes from Evenki; shamans journey to celestial and underground realms to rescue souls and heal; 123,423 people in Russia's 2002 census belonged to groups mainly following traditional beliefs. The world tree is not covered by the checked source.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siberian_shamanism

mgs|part|Böö (shaman) from early Mongolian böge; female shamans tied to Etügen, Mother Earth. Ovoo and the post-1990 revival are not covered by the checked source.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siberian_shamanism

sam|part|The noaidi mediated with the underworld using a drum; sieidi sacred stones; reindeer offerings; practised until the 18th c. The modern revival is not covered by the checked source.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%C3%A1mi_shamanism;https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siberian_shamanism

fin|fix|Ukko, Tuonela and oral runo songs (written down as the Kalevala by Lönnrot) confirmed. Forbidden from the 1600s, but sacred groves were used in the 1700s, beliefs mixed with Christianity into the 19th c. and folk magic lasted to the early 20th c. End moved from 1700 to 1850.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_paganism

suo|fix|A 20th-c. reconstruction that gained official minority-religion status in 2013; the registered community Karhun kansa had about 80 members in 2020. Description updated.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finnish_paganism
ain|ok|Kamuy in all of nature; iyomante bear-sending (banned 1955, revived as an annual festival); inau offerings; settlements of the 13th–17th c.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ainu_religion

inu|part|Angakkuit (men and women); Sedna withholds sea mammals when taboos are broken; animal souls must be respected. Paleo-Eskimo dating is not covered by the checked source.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inuit_religion

san|fix|Trance dance (women clap and sing, men dance) after initiation through a power animal such as the eland; ǀKágge̥n the Mantis trickster-demiurge; Drakensberg paintings c. 3,000 years old with religious meaning. The 'distant creator' ǃXu is likely a missionary-influenced figure, so the sky-god trait was removed and the rock-art age claim softened.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_religion

nil|ok|Dinka Nhialic, the distant sky and rain creator (Jaak/Juong among the Nuer and Shilluk); cattle sacrifice with prayer; jok ancestral spirits and patron powers.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinka_religion
mas|unv|Not covered by the checked source; standard references.|

waq|fix|Waaqa is the supreme creator (the source does not call him a sky god, so that trait was removed); Qaalluu priests uphold Gadaa; the Irreecha thanksgiving at Lake Hora Harsedi draws millions. Active practitioners are estimated at c. 1.1 million, with other estimates up to 5 million.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waaqeffanna

bwi|fix|Practised by the Punu, Mitsogo and Fang of Gabon and said to originate among Pygmy (Mbenge) groups; iboga initiation is the crucial rite; often syncretized with Catholicism; honors ancestors. No founding date: iboga has been used 'for hundreds of years', so start moved to 1600 at low confidence.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bwiti

brb|ok|Amun with his oracle at Siwa, Tanit, Gurzil (temple at Ghirza used into the 6th c.), Ifri; dream incubation at ancestral tombs (Herodotus); persisted among tribes into the 7th c. and faded after the Arab conquest.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_Berber_religion
gch|part|Guanches mummified their dead, unlike most mainland Berbers. Achamán is not covered by the checked source.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_Berber_religion

teo|ok|Founded c. 100 BCE, sacked c. 550 CE; the Great Goddess as primary deity, plus the Storm God and Feathered Serpent; sacrificial burials consecrating the Feathered Serpent temple c. 200 CE; the Aztecs later revered the site as the place where the gods were born.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teotihuacan
moc|ok|c. 100–800 CE; human sacrifice central in art; Lord of Sipán (found 1987) and Lady of Cao (2005), suggesting priestess-queens.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moche_culture

tiw|fix|Founded c. 110 CE (radiocarbon), peaked c. 500–600 and collapsed around 1000, so start moved from 500 to 110. The Gateway of the Sun Staff God is variously identified with Viracocha or Tunuupa; sacrificial dedications at the Akapana; a pilgrimage centre at the 'centre of the universe'.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiwanaku

hop|part|Hopewell 100 BCE–500 CE: mounds with exotic grave goods for important people, geometric earthworks (Newark Octagon, a possible lunar observatory) and ceremonial centres. The Adena start date is not covered by the checked source.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hopewell_tradition

pue|fix|Masked kachina dances as prayer (over 500 kachinas), the kiva, and balance for rain. Cliff dwellings date to c. 900–1350, and the source says the religion likely took shape in the late 13th–early 14th c., so start moved from 750 to 1300. The emergence myth is not covered by the checked source.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pueblo_religion

iro|part|Sky Woman falls from the sky island and gives birth to twins, the good Sapling (Hah-gweh-di-yu) and destructive Flint, which fits the dual-creation trait; spring thanksgiving dances. The Great Law of Peace, Thanksgiving Address and Green Corn rites are not covered by the checked source.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haudenosaunee_mythology

mpc|fix|The machi (mostly women) heals and divines, climbing the rewe pole (an axis mundi) in trance flight; the ngillatun community prayer includes offerings and animal sacrifice. The name Ngünechen for the main deity is attested from the 19th c. In 2001, 8% followed traditional religion only. Sacrifice and world-axis traits added.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mapuche_religion

sdm|ok|Founded by Raimundo Irineu Serra in Acre in the 1920s–30s; ayahuasca (Daime) as sacrament; hymns (O Cruzeiro); folk Catholic and Kardecist Spiritist elements. Barquinha and UDV are allied ayahuasca churches.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santo_Daime
brq|part|Named as an allied ayahuasca church of Santo Daime; date from standard references.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santo_Daime

tai|ok|Zemís as deities or ancestral spirits and the objects housing them; creator Yúcahu and fertility goddess Atabey; ancestors' bones kept in zemís and given offerings; medicine people consulted zemís for healing.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zemi

msc|fix|Sué (sun) and Chía (moon), Bochica, and Chibchacum (rain, offered gold); gold and emerald offerings at sacred lakes such as Guatavita fed the El Dorado legend. The last public ceremony was on 27 December 1563 at Ubaque, so end moved from 1600 to 1563.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muisca_religion

nwc|part|The potlatch gift feast (Haida, Tlingit, Kwakwaka'wakw, Coast Salish and others) honors the supernatural and ancestral lineages; secret-society dances (hamatsa); banned in Canada from 1884/85 until 1951. Guardian spirits and totem poles are not covered by the checked source.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potlatch

wix|ok|Annual peyote (hikuri) pilgrimage to Wirikuta; Corn, Blue Deer and Peyote descend from the Sun God; Rain Goddess; shamanic practice largely survived colonial pressure.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huichol

smu|fix|First reported by anthropologists in 1940s Mexico City (Tepito); went public when Enriqueta Romero opened a street shrine in 2001; condemned by the Catholic Church and denounced by Pope Francis in 2016; about 12 million devotees (2016–17). Scholars debate any link to the Aztec death goddess Mictēcacihuātl. Description updated.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Muerte

mfc|ok|Day of the Dead blends Mesoamerican rites with Catholic All Saints and All Souls; home ofrendas; inscribed by UNESCO in 2008. Scholars debate the balance of the two sources.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day_of_the_Dead

and|part|Quyllurit'i is a syncretic Andean–Catholic pilgrimage near Cusco (UNESCO 2011), with a Catholic founding story from 1783 and pre-Columbian ties to the Pleiades. Apus and Pachamama offerings are not covered by the checked source.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quyllur_Rit%27i

drm|fix|Smohalla (c. 1815–1895), a Wanapum prophet, revived the Washani religion and Washat dance from about 1850, urging a return to ancestral ways under God and Mother Earth. The source does not mention his rejection of farming, so the description was reworded.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smohalla

haw|ok|Kū, Kāne, Lono and Kanaloa; heiau temples with offerings and human sacrifice; Makahiki season for Lono with the Kumulipo chant; the kapu system was overthrown in 1819 by Liholiho, Kaʻahumanu and Keōpūolani with the high priest Hewahewa; revival from the 1970s Hawaiian Renaissance.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaiian_religion

rap|part|Moai as deified ancestors facing inland; the later birdman cult of Makemake; declined after conversion to Catholicism. Exact dates and Orongo are not covered by the checked source.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapa_Nui_mythology

rat|ok|T. W. Rātana's vision on 8 November 1918 began a healing mission; the church was formally established in 1925, its temple opened in 1928, and it allied with Labour (formally 1936). Beliefs centre on the Trinity, the Faithful Angels and Te Māngai. 43,821 adherents in the 2018 census.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R%C4%81tana

pmr|fix|Te Ua Haumēne's revelation in September 1862; flourished 1863–1874 amid the New Zealand Wars; blended Old Testament morality with Māori spirituality, observed the Sabbath and held rites at the niu pole; 609 adherents in 2006. Elements were absorbed into Ringatū (1868). Sabbath trait and Ringatū link added.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pai_M%C4%81rire

mel|part|Ancestor spirits (tamate) and ghost tales; culture heroes Qat, To-Kabinana and Tagaro; cargo cults arose in the 20th c. Initiation cults and exchange with spirits are not covered by the checked source.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melanesian_mythology
fij|part|Fijian myth of the serpent Ndengei (Degei), who hatches two children from eggs.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melanesian_mythology

kej|ok|Javanism (kebatinan) blends animist, Hindu-Buddhist (from c. 1st c. CE) and Islamic, including Sufi, elements, with Islam adopted around 1500; it seeks inner harmony and union through meditation, fasting and tapa. Recognized in 1973 as a 'belief in One God', not a religion.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kejawen
sbd|ok|Subud was founded in the 1920s by Muhammad Subuh, within Javanese kebatinan.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kejawen

khr|fix|Dayak folk religion of Central and South Kalimantan with the Panaturan scripture; the 30-day Tiwah second funeral with animal sacrifice. Grouped under Hindu Dharma from 1980 and recognized as an indigenous belief (Aliran Kepercayaan) since November 2017; about 330,000 adherents. Description updated.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaharingan

mal|part|Famadihana: every five to seven years families exhume and rewrap ancestors and dance with them; possibly only since the 17th c. in its present form, adapting older Austronesian double-funeral customs. Zanahary and fady are not covered by the checked source.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Famadihana

fil|ok|Anito are ancestor and nature spirits and deities; babaylan (mostly women) enter trance and are possessed in pag-anito séances; devotion transferred to patron saints in folk Catholicism; Bathala as chief Tagalog deity.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anito

srn|fix|Followed by Santal, Oraon, Ho and Munda; communal offerings twice a year in sacred groves (sarna) led by pahan priests; deities Gram Deota, Marang Buru, Singbonga and the earth mother Chalapachho Devi ('Dharmes' is not in the source, so removed); 4,957,467 followers in the 2011 census; activists seek a separate census code.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarnaism

dnp|fix|A revivalist movement among the Adi and other Tani peoples venerating Donyi (Mother Sun) and Polo (Father Moon); the revival began after a 1968 meeting and was formalized in 1986 (Donyi-Polo Yelam Kebang) by Talom Rukbo; about 363,000 followers in 2011. Scholars see the organized form as a 20th-c. development, so it is now dated 1968 as a modern revival of older Tani traditions.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donyi-Polo

snm|ok|Ethnic polytheism of the Meitei named after Lainingthou Sanamahi; amaiba and amaibi priests under the Maru Loishang; Lai Haraoba festival with possessed priestesses; revival from 1930 (Apokpa Marup); 222,422 adherents in 2011.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanamahism

klh|ok|Animism and ancestor worship with ancient Indo-Iranian, Vedic-like gods (Dezau the creator, Imra, Indr, Mahandeo, Jeṣṭak, Sajigor); goat sacrifice; dehar shamans; strict purity rules (bashaleni); Chilam Joshi, Uchau and Chaumos festivals; 7,466 Kalasha speakers (2023 census).|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalash_people
nrs|ok|Neighbouring Nuristanis, who shared a similar archaic faith, were forcibly converted to Islam in 1895–96.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalash_people

nwt|fix|King Anawrahta (1044–1077) formalized the 37 nats under Thagyamin after failing to suppress nat worship. Nats include humans deified after death and nature spirits (not only the 'tragic dead'); nat-kadaw mediums are possessed and dance at nat-pwe festivals alongside Buddhist practice. Taungbyone is not covered by the checked source, so it was removed.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burmese_folk_religion

krt|ok|Followed by Rai, Limbu, Yakkha, Sunuwar and others; the oral Mundhum serves as myth, ritual and customary law; shamanism and ancestor and nature worship; nakchhong and phedangma priests; 924,204 adherents (3.17%) in Nepal's 2021 census.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirat_Mundhum

bth|ok|Bodo folk religion of the unseen supreme deity Bathoubwrai, embodied in the sijou plant at the household altar; Mainao protects the rice fields; Kherai festival; douri and doudini priests, with a revival by the All Bathou Religious Union (1992).|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bathouism

hrk|fix|Founded in the late 1920s by Haipou Jadonang (executed 1931) and led afterward by Rani Gaidinliu; a monotheistic reform of the Zeliangrong Naga faith, worshipping Tingwang exclusively in Kelumki prayer houses; about 25,000–30,000 followers. Start moved from 1930 to 1927.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heraka

phi|ok|Tai folk religion of phi spirits, khwan (vital essences) and ancestors; guardian spirits of temples, towns, villages and houses; miniature spirit shrines; mophi shamans. It blends with Buddhism; about 30% of Lao reportedly follow it, though it is not officially recognized.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satsana_Phi
ahr|ok|The Ahom form (Ban Phi) with Molung priestly clans.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satsana_Phi

kns|part|Niam Khasi is the monotheistic indigenous faith centred on U Blei Nongthaw, the formless creator, followed by 15.41% of Khasis (2011). The Seng Khasi founding date (1899) is not covered by the checked source.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khasi_people

hmg|ok|Shamans (spirit-chosen men or women) heal with ua neeb rites; soul-calling (hu plig) restores lost soul parts; each person has many souls, one of which is reborn; ancestors receive food, spirit money and incense; the household altar (Thaj Neeb).|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hmong_customs_and_culture

vdd|fix|A 'cult of the dead': ancestral nae yaku are invoked for hunting, with the kirikoraha offering to the newly dead and a unique deity, Kande Yakka; blended with nominal Buddhism or Hinduism; the Kataragama shrine is shared. Possession and dance are not described in the checked source, so those traits were removed.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vedda

tbp|fix|Ancient bon priests appeased spirits, guided the dead, sacrificed animals and buried the dead with jewels; a court religion legitimized the Yarlung kings with sacrificial, oracular and shamanic rites (dated by Thurman to c. 100 BCE under Pudegungyal). Start moved from 500 BCE to 100 BCE.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibetan_folk_religion

bon|ok|Yungdrung Bön emerged in the 10th–11th c. with Shenchen Luga's early-11th-c. treasure discoveries; Menri Monastery founded 1405; c. 400,000 followers on the Tibetan Plateau (2019). Scholars debate how much is pre-Buddhist.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibetan_folk_religion

bli|ok|Shiva-centred worship with Buddhist elements and Austronesian ancestor veneration; Sang Hyang Widhi Wasa; daily canang sari offerings; odalan temple festivals and Galungan every 210 days; ngaben cremation. About 3.8 million adherents. Legend credits Rsi Markandeya (8th c.), with Majapahit conquest in 1343 and Nirartha's reforms from 1492.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bali_Hinduism

lus|fix|Developed in western Cuba in the late 19th c. from Yoruba religion, Catholicism and Spiritism, so start moved from 1800 to 1870. Oricha paired with saints (Changó with Santa Bárbara, Ochún with Our Lady of Charity); kariocha initiation; Ifá babalawos; batá drumming calls oricha to possess participants; animal sacrifice; Lucumí ritual language; high hundreds of thousands of initiates.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santer%C3%ADa

pal|fix|A Kongo-derived religion that developed in Cuba in the late 19th or early 20th c., so start moved from 1800 to 1890. The nganga vessel holds the dead (nfumbe); Nsambi is a remote creator; mpungu spirits; branches Mayombe, Monte, Briyumba and Kimbisa.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palo_(religion)

wnt|ok|Blends Akan, Fon and Kongo beliefs brought by enslaved Africans; winti spirits created by the supreme Anana in earth, water, forest and sky pantheons; possession; outlawed from 1874 until 1971.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winti

kmn|ok|19th-c. Jamaica (St Thomas), from Kongo-region indentured labourers after abolition; spirit possession for healing; its drumming shaped Nyabinghi and reggae.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kumina

spb|fix|In Trinidad it traces to Merikins (formerly enslaved Americans who fought for Britain in 1812) settled c. 1815–16, so start moved from 1850 to 1816. Banned by the Shouter Prohibition Ordinance 1917–1951; Liberation Day (30 March) a public holiday since 1996; invoking the Holy Spirit; coloured gowns and headties.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spiritual_Baptist

qmb|fix|Grew out of the broader Macumba complex as the 'sibling' of Umbanda (1920s Rio), taking what Umbanda rejected; centred on Exus and Pombagiras ('spirits of the left'), with rituals at crossroads, sometimes involving animal sacrifice; grew strongly from the 1970s. Start moved from 1950 to 1930 and description reworded.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quimbanda

tdm|ok|Mainly practised in Maranhão, Piauí, Pará and the Amazon; Casa das Minas in São Luís was founded in the 1840s; Fon (Jeje) vodun and encantados; songs in Ewe-Fon.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tambor_de_Mina

abk|ok|A Cuban men's initiatory fraternity derived from the Ékpè society of the Cross River region; first lodge formed in Regla in 1836; controlled much of Cuban port labour from the 1870s to 1942.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abaku%C3%A1

mli|fix|Goddess of nature, love and harmony, centred on Sorte Mountain (pilgrimage every 12 October); spirit courts (Indigenous, African, Viking, Liberator) including Guaicaipuro, Negro Felipe and Bolívar; mediums lead devotees into trance. A 20th-c. blend; the Sorte rituals are dated to the early 1920s, so start moved from 1900 to 1920.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mar%C3%ADa_Lionza

sgd|ok|Founded in the 7th c. with En no Gyōja as patriarch; yamabushi mountain ascetics; a syncretic mix of Esoteric Buddhism, Shinto, mountain worship and Taoism; banned in 1872 and revived after WWII.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shugend%C5%8D

cdo|ok|Choe Je-u began Donghak in 1860 as an alternative to 'Western Learning'; serving a person is serving Heaven (Haneullim); the 1894 peasant rebellion; renamed Cheondoism by Son Byong-hi on 1 December 1905; about 65,000 adherents (2015 census).|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheondoism

jsn|part|Followers regard Kang Jeungsan (d. 1909) as the incarnation of Sangje, the Supreme God; an umbrella for more than 100 movements, including Bocheon-gyo (claimed about 6 million in the 1920s) and Jeung San Do (1974). The 1901 revelation date is not covered by the checked source.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeungsanism

dsj|ok|Founded in 1969 by Park Wudang, successor of Jo Jeongsan's Mugeukdo (1925); apparently the largest Jeungsanist group; split after Park's death in 1996.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeungsanism

mzu|ok|Lin Moniang of Meizhou Island, a shamaness deified after her death (dated 987), protector of seafarers and later 'Queen of Heaven'; about 1,500 temples in 26 countries, roughly 1,000 of them in Taiwan; Dajia and Baishatun pilgrimages.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mazuism

dmu|fix|Established in the 16th c., so start moved from 1500 to 1550; inscribed by UNESCO in December 2016. In the hầu bóng ceremony the medium stays in control and deities do not enter the body, so the possession trait was removed and the description reworded.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C4%90%E1%BA%A1o_M%E1%BA%ABu

djj|ok|Founded in Seoul in 1909 by Na Cheol (1864–1916) as Dangunism, renamed a year later; Dangun is seen as the human manifestation of a trinitarian God, Haneullim; a focus of the independence movement in Manchuria; about 400,000 followers in the 1910s but fewer than 10,000 in the 1995 census.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daejongism

kkg|fix|An Edo-period 'national learning' turning from Chinese, Confucian and Buddhist texts to early Japanese classics, traditionally founded by Kada no Azumamaro (1669–1736), with Kamo no Mabuchi, Motoori Norinaga and Hirata Atsutane; it fed State Shinto and sonnō jōi. Start moved from 1760 to 1700.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kokugaku

izm|fix|Established in 1882 by Senge Takatomi (1845–1918), 80th head priest of Izumo-taisha; its predecessor dates to 1873. Ōkuninushi is the head kami. One of the original thirteen sect Shinto groups. Start moved from 1873 to 1882.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izumo-taishakyo

kcc|ok|Proposed by Kang Youwei and founded by Chen Huanzhang in 1912, with 132 branches before 1920s anti-religious campaigns dissolved it on the mainland. It continues through Hong Kong's Confucian Academy and an Indonesian supreme council.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confucian_church

tao|ok|The Daodejing existed by the 3rd c. BCE, perhaps growing from oral sayings; the Laozi legend developed in the Han and has no historical validity; wu wei and the unnamable Dao; commentaries by Wang Bi and Guo Xiang.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taoist_philosophy

ysd|ok|Created by Yoshida Kanetomo (1435–1511) in the Sengoku period as 'One-and-only Shintō', reversing honji suijaku so that Buddhist deities are manifestations of kami; the 1665 regulations made the Yoshida supervisors of lesser shrines until the late Edo period.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoshida_Shint%C5%8D

nss|ok|Head temple Taiseki-ji established 1290 by Nikkō (1246–1333); Nichiren honored as the True Buddha; the Dai Gohonzon; Soka Gakkai was its lay organization until excommunicated on 28 November 1991; claims over 800,000 members.|https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nichiren_Sh%C5%8Dsh%C5%AB
